transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Alex Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Platform) -- Jon Mercer (Lunaris ML Eng), Sara Kim (Lunaris Infra), Diego Alvarez (Lunaris SRE), Elena Park (Lunaris DS)

Auto-summary (auto): intermittent KV evictions when long-context prompts with varying tokenization hit model; suspected prefetch heuristic + prefix aliasing.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, do we have audio and video ok?
[00:12] Jon: yeah can hear ya, good to go
[00:16] Alex: cool, quick agenda, reproduce the thrash, look at prefetch heuristics, tokenization mismatch, then mitigation options (quantization fallback, prefetch tuning, eviction backoff)
[00:30] Sara: we see latency spikes ~200-400ms extra per request and occasional 5-8s tails, not sure if that line up with your SLOs but it kills UX
[00:45] Maya: yup, thanks. Jon, can you describe how you trigger the long-context calls?
[00:58] Jon: sure, our chat flows append a 6-8k token user history, then we do a rerank step and finally a long generation step, so sequence length varies. We also have mixed tokenizers - legacy tokenizers for some legacy pipelines and new SentencePiece for others, so prefix hashes sometimes differ
[01:20] Elena: and we saw KV entries not reused across those because the prefix key was different; it looked like prefix shadowing to us
[01:35] Alex: prefix shadowing, yep that rings a bell. On Redwood side we track prefix keys at tokenize-time; if different tokenization yields different token ids, KV won't hit. Did you try normalizing tokens at the caller?
[01:50] Jon: we did some normalization but not consistent across services; also quantized variants do a different byte-level token layout apparently which may change the effective key
[02:10] Diego: The SREs also noted spillover events: GPU free memory dips and then the runtime starts paging KV blobs to local disk which increases latency then the KV eviction churn increases - looks like a feedback loop
[02:35] Priya: interesting, the runtime's adaptive paging threshold can be tuned; default is 70% mem util before spill. If your mix has sudden bursts, that could trigger thrashing. But we need to correlate exact timestamps
[02:55] Maya: Alex, can you sketch the reproducer approach?
[03:03] Alex: yeah, plan is: run staged load with mixed tokenization, synthetic long-context prompts two sizes (4k, 8k), interleave small quick queries to exercise prefix reuse, enable KV debug tracing, collect KV hit/miss, eviction reasons, and kernel scheduling traces. We'll also instrument the quantized vs fp16 variant behavior. That should show whether tokenization or prefetching is dominant cause
[03:32] Jon: sounds good. on tokenization we have an example where the same sentence produced two different prefix hashes across services, i'll share that example
[03:45] Elena: note: some of our logs mask tokens for PII so we can't always compare raw tokens; may need to attach token IDs instead of raw text
[04:02] Alex: yep, token IDs are perfect. Also capture KV prefix lengths and the stored meta (last accessed time).
[04:18] Sara: question: if the runtime spills KV to disk, is it encrypted under their KMS? we run in a VPC private deployment
[04:28] Priya: yes, for Private deployments disk spill uses customer-managed KMS when configured; we can confirm key rotation behavior but data-at-rest is encrypted. Redwood only needs read access to logs (RO) for triage
[04:45] Diego: another observation: bursting requests during model switchovers (canary -> full) caused compaction cycles. Is there an automatic backoff to reduce prefetch in low-memory?
[04:58] Alex: we have an eviction backoff that reduces aggressive prefetch when eviction rate > X. But default X is tuned for cloud-hosted patterns; in private deploys with different memory shapes you might want lower prefetch aggressiveness
[05:20] Jon: can you explain prefix reuse vs prefix aliasing? sometimes reuse should happen but it doesn't
[05:30] Alex: short answer: reuse requires identical token id sequence and same kv namespace. aliasing happens when users do lightweight normalization but still produce different ids. Also sequence offsets matter - prefix reuse typically uses a canonical prefix anchor (session id + prompt hash). If either changes, we store separate prefixes.
[05:55] Elena: in our logs we saw many small prefixes with high overlap but different hashes - so storage bloat and more eviction pressure. Is there a recombine/compaction mechanism?
[06:10] Priya: there's a compaction job that dedups similar prefixes offline, but it needs heuristics and is not enabled by default in private by default because it can be expensive. We can enable for staging to test impact
[06:30] Diego: can compaction happen online when memory is tight?
[06:36] Alex: online compaction is risky; it adds CPU and can momentarily increase memory. We favor eviction heuristics and smarter prefetching first
[06:48] Jon: any quick mitigations we can try?
[06:52] Maya: yes, short term: 1) normalize tokenization at caller, 2) lower prefetch aggressiveness, 3) exclude very short high-turn prefixes from caching, 4) enable KV debug and run reproducer
[07:10] Jon: on tokenization normalization — that will require small changes but doable
[07:18] Elena: question about quantized model differences — does quantization change tokenization? we noticed token boundaries shifted on some runs
[07:27] Alex: quantization shouldn't change tokenization generally but model variant differences (token embedding tables sharded differently or tokenizer versions packaged with the model) can lead to mismatches. Packaging conventions sometimes bundle tokenizer files with the model artifact which causes drift if deployments use different artifact versions
[07:50] Sara: we are on private deployment, we control artifacts but some older microservices are still hitting hosted endpoints with a slightly different model artifact. Could that create the misaligned prefixes?
[08:02] Priya: yes, if hosted and private variants use different tokenizer versions, prefix hashes will diverge. We recommend pinning tokenizer versions in the deployment manifest
[08:18] Diego: about the paging impact: when spill happens does the runtime evict hot prefixes first or oldest? We saw hot items being evicted, which is counterintuitive
[08:31] Alex: eviction policy is LRU with hotness boost; but if the metadata (last-access timestamps) are inaccurate due to clock skew across nodes or batched updates, hotness signals can be stale leading to wrong evictions. We'll check your node clocks and the batched oom handling config
[08:55] Jon: we do have a small clock skew on one node (~500ms) per our monitoring, could that be enough?
[09:03] Alex: yes, it can affect ordering in LRU windows. Also batched last-access updates can be delayed under heavy load, increasing chance of thrash
[09:18] Maya: we'll include clock sync checks in the reproducer runbook
[09:25] Elena: any thoughts on batching effects? our throughput is limited so we batch to reduce cost but latency spikes correlate with batch formation and KV misses
[09:38] Alex: batching increases per-request token processing windows and can cause cache pressure because the runtime prefetches tokens for entire batch; if the batch has diverse prefixes, you get more unique KV entries referenced, causing more memory pressure. Consider request-affinity batching (group by prefix) or smaller batch windows for mixed workloads
[10:00] Jon: request-affinity batching might be hard on our side but possible as middleware routing. Could Redwood do affinity in the router?
[10:10] Priya: router-level affinity is feasible; we can add a sticky batching policy keyed on prefix hash for Dedicated/private deployments. That reduces cross-prefix mixing in a batch
[10:25] Diego: about telemetry, can we get per-prefix eviction rates and mem footprint?
[10:31] Alex: yes, we can emit per-prefix metrics (sampled) and an aggregated eviction/insert rate. We'll share a dashboard link. Expect sampling to be on by default; for full fidelity we need debug mode which is more verbose
[10:48] Maya: okay let's pivot to reproducer assignment, Alex will craft it and attach the exact commands and env variables
[10:56] Alex: reproducer will be a kube job for staging: two worker pods, instrumented load generator, token ID capture, KV debug = true, mem watermarks set to mimic prod. We'll also include an alternate run with lowered prefetch and another with online compaction enabled
[11:18] Sara: for the staging run can Redwood temporarily enable compaction?
[11:23] Priya: yes for staging only, we can run compaction for a 2-hour window, monitor impact and revert. We'll coordinate windows
[11:33] Jon: will that compaction produce significant cpu? we run on constrained machines
[11:39] Alex: it will use CPU but we can throttle. We'll provide knob recommendations
[11:49] Elena: any perf numbers you can share from other customers who saw similar patterns?
[11:54] Maya: anonymized: Customer X saw 30% drop in eviction rate after lowering prefetch and enabling affinity; median P95 latency improved from 1.4s to 720ms in one week. Not identical workloads but gives a signal
[12:12] Diego: on security — can Redwood read debug logs in private if we give RO access? we want to maintain data residency
[12:20] Priya: yes you can grant scoped read-only log access; we don't exfiltrate, we operate under your IAM and audit logs show every action. We'll share our security pack (SOC2, data flows)
[12:35] Jon: please include an explicit list of log fields you need so we can mask PII before sharing
[12:41] Alex: will do, token IDs and hashes are enough, no raw text required
[12:47] Maya: quick recap: Redwood to deliver reproducer + instrumentation, share telemetry dashboard links and knob recommendations; Lunaris to run reproducer and enable debug logs; follow-up on 2025-04-10. Action items listed in chat
[13:05] Elena: thanks everyone, this was useful
[13:10] Jon: thanks, appreciate it
[13:14] Maya: bye all

References/links discussed: console KV dashboard (link: https://console.redwood.ai/kvdash/CRM-77412), reproducer template (doc stub shared in chat), security pack (link note: redwood-security-pack.pdf)
